q: I'm standing on a mountain top. How is Isa connected to Gebo?
text: At the top there is nowhere further up, and the climbing stops being something you do. Isa is that halt. The wind has dropped; the snow on the summit fell long ago and has not shifted since. Everything the ascent took out of your legs is up here with you, held in the cold, and Gebo stands half-finished: the giving has gone one way, and the other half lies under the snow, frozen exactly where it was given.

q: I'm standing on a mountain top. What is my life rune's relationship in the Isa picture?
text: On the summit your life rune is the part that keeps count. Isa has stopped everything else up here — the wind, the snow, the climb itself — but Gebo does not stop; it only waits for a return. You carried the whole height up in your legs, and the mountain has taken it without handing anything back. The summit holds the climb the way cold holds breath: kept, not spent, and not answered.

q: I'm standing on a mountain top. Enrich the Isa picture with my life rune.
text: On the summit the old snow carries a second set of tracks, coming up the far side of the ridge and stopping a few steps from yours. Isa keeps both exactly where they ended. Nobody crosses the last few steps, and nothing moves between the two sets of prints. Gebo lives in that strip of untouched snow: two arrivals facing each other, each one a gift the other has not yet taken.

q: I'm standing on a mountain top. What is the relationship between Isa and Gebo in the picture?
text: In this picture Isa is the summit's stillness and Gebo is the climb you brought to it. The relationship is a halt in the middle of an exchange: you gave the mountain every step of the way up, and the mountain has taken it into its cold without returning anything. Neither side has broken the balance — the giving has simply been frozen before it could come back.

q: I'm standing on a mountain top. How does Gebo reach into the Isa picture?
text: Gebo reaches in from below. Far down the slope, where the snow ends and the rock begins, the path you climbed is still warm from your walking, and the summit is not. Between the two runs the whole height: what you spent going up lies below, what the mountain holds lies here, and the cold keeps them from meeting. Isa keeps the summit still; Gebo is the pull between the top and the path, reaching up and not arriving.

q: I'm standing on a mountain top. What passes between me and this place?
text: Very little moves between you. You brought the climb up here, all of it, and the summit has taken it the way cold takes heat — slowly, and without any sign that it noticed. Isa holds the top in a stillness that does not trade. What passes between you and this place is only the breath leaving you and the air not moving to meet it.

q: I'm standing on a mountain top. What does my own way of going change here?
text: On the summit your way of going meets something that will not go back and forth. You climb by meeting the slope halfway, step for step, and up here there is no slope left to meet. Isa has taken the other half of every exchange out of reach: the stone does not push back, the wind has dropped, the snow asks nothing. Your going has nothing to lean against, so it stops — not from tiredness, but because nothing answers.

q: I'm looking into the distance at a flying bird. How is Perth connected to Gebo?
text: The bird is too far off to name. You can follow the line it draws across the sky, but not where that line began or where it will come down, and what it carries is a dark point too small to make out. Perth is the part of the flight kept from you. Gebo is the flight itself: something is being taken from one place to another, and you are watching the middle of the handing-over, with both ends out of sight.

q: I'm looking into the distance at a flying bird. What is my life rune's relationship in the Perth picture?
text: In the Perth picture your life rune is the reason the bird holds your eye. It is carrying something from one place to another, and you can see neither end — but you can see that it is carrying. That is Gebo's part: the handing-over is real even while its sender and receiver stay hidden. Perth keeps the ends from you. Your life rune keeps your eye on the middle.

q: I'm looking into the distance at a flying bird. Enrich the Perth picture with my life rune.
text: The bird lets something fall — a small dark fleck that drops away from it and is lost against the slope below. A second bird, lower down, swings out to where it fell. Perth keeps both too far away for you to say what was dropped or whether it was meant to be caught. Gebo is in the fall between them: one letting go, one turning toward it, and what passes between them never visible.

q: I'm looking into the distance at a flying bird. What is the relationship between Perth and Gebo in the picture?
text: In this picture Perth and Gebo are two halves of the same flight. Gebo is the exchange — something is being carried from one place and delivered to another. Perth is what hides that exchange from you: you see the bird, but not the giver it left or the hands it is flying toward. The relationship is a gift in transit, visible only in its middle.

q: I'm looking into the distance at a flying bird. How does Gebo reach into the Perth picture?
text: Gebo reaches in along the line of flight. The bird did not start where you first saw it; it came from somewhere behind the ridge, and it is going somewhere past the far edge of the sky. Perth hides both of those places. What Gebo adds is only direction — the sense that the flight is a carrying and not a wandering, pointed from one hand-over toward the next.

q: I'm looking into the distance at a flying bird. What passes between me and that bird?
text: Only your looking. The bird does not turn, does not change its line, and does not know it is being followed across the whole width of the sky. Perth keeps it too far off to read. What goes from you to the bird is attention; what comes back is the shape of its flight, getting smaller.

q: I'm looking into the distance at a flying bird. What does my own way of going change here?
text: Standing still to watch a bird is not how your going usually works; it moves by meeting things halfway, and a bird in the distance cannot be met at all. Perth keeps its path hidden, so there is no halfway to find — the line runs out of sight at both ends. Your going has to settle for following with the eyes, giving attention and getting back only the flight itself.
